title: Lecture 02 - Non-relational databases and Slack's real-time communication

questions.q: What were the two parts of this session's agenda, and what restriction was put on the second one?
questions.answer: First half: non-relational databases (an overview, including where NOT to use them). Second half: designing Slack's real-time communication, text-based only.

questions.q: What did the teacher say the Slack design would show about other chat products such as WhatsApp and Zoom chat?
questions.answer: The same design can switch from one message-delivery model to another just by changing the guarantees, so Slack, WhatsApp and Zoom chat are all variations of one architecture (system design is about recognising patterns / Lego blocks).

questions.q: Why did the teacher dislike the blanket terms 'NoSQL' or 'non-relational' and the claim 'NoSQL databases scale'?
questions.answer: Because they lump everything that is not MySQL/Postgres/Oracle together; you should name the specific type of database. And you can build a non-relational database that does not scale at all, so 'NoSQL scales' is wrong as a blanket statement.

questions.q: As a very broad (not always true) distinction, what do non-relational databases typically give up, and what do they get in exchange?
questions.answer: They typically give up (strong) consistency to gain scalability (horizontal scaling) and availability.

questions.q: The teacher said there are two kinds of 'consistency'. What are they, and which one is meant when saying NoSQL databases give up consistency?
questions.answer: ACID consistency: data moves from one correct state to another (correctness). CAP consistency: data being visible/available to query right away after a write (strong vs eventual). The NoSQL trade-off refers to the CAP kind.

questions.q: Why is a classic relational database less available than a horizontally spread non-relational one, and what consistency model do most NoSQL databases end up with?
questions.answer: A relational database keeps all the data in one instance, so if it goes down the system is down. Non-relational databases spread data over multiple nodes, so others serve data when one fails. Most NoSQL DBs are eventually consistent (board: 'Most NoSQL DBs are eventually consistent').

questions.q: What did the pink box on the board say about whether SQL databases scale, and what example from the previous class backed it up?
questions.answer: 'NoSQL DBs scale does not mean SQL does not' -> 'anything that shards, scales'. The previous class sharded a key-value store on a relational DB (keys A-M on one DB, N-Z on another), giving up consistency for horizontal scalability.

questions.q: What attitude did the teacher ask students to take towards generic statements about technology (even his own)?
questions.answer: Never believe a generic statement at face value; it must be specific and contextual. Ask critical questions, because you can always find a counter-example.

questions.q: List the four properties of document databases written on the board and the two examples given.
questions.answer: Mostly JSON based; supports complex queries; partial updates to documents possible; closest to relational databases. Examples: MongoDB, Elasticsearch.

questions.q: When companies move a generic relational schema to a non-relational database, which type do they typically adopt, and why not a key-value store?
questions.answer: A document database, because it gives almost the features a relational DB gave. A key-value store is too restrictive: you cannot look inside the value.

questions.q: What does 'partial update' mean in a document database, and what must you do instead in a key-value store whose value is a blob?
questions.answer: You can query on a document's attributes and update just one attribute in place. With a blob value you must read, update and write back the whole value.

questions.q: What example showed that the line between document databases and key-value stores is blurry, and what should an engineer focus on instead of the category?
questions.answer: DynamoDB is a key-value store yet lets you query within the document. Focus on the access pattern and the features you need, and which database gives them.

questions.q: What example showed that generic claims about a database can become false over time?
questions.answer: MongoDB used to say 'we are BASE, not ACID', but now MongoDB is ACID compliant (though perhaps not as optimal as SQL).

questions.q: What operations does a key-value store allow, and what examples were written on the board?
questions.answer: Only key-wise operations: get, put, delete, insert a key (or insert a value into a set represented by a key). Examples: Redis, DynamoDB, Aerospike.

questions.q: Why can a key-value store be partitioned into thousands of partitions, while richer query models cannot?
questions.answer: Every operation is on a single key, so there are never cross-shard queries. Range/IN queries (e.g. IDs 1,2,3 on three different DBs) need cross-shard queries, which are expensive, so the more complex the queries the less you can distribute the data.

questions.q: State the trade-off of key-value stores (board: two bullets added under 'Key Value store').
questions.answer: Heavily partitioned (massive parallelism, availability, performance) but no complex queries supported: you lose query power and gain parallelism.

questions.q: What example table was used for column-oriented databases, and what were its columns?
questions.answer: stock_ticks: Symbol, price, name, exchange, timestamp (one entry per stock tick).

questions.q: In the row-oriented vs column-oriented drawing, how are rows R1-R3 laid out in each store?
questions.answer: Row store: each row is one long rectangle of 5 cells stored contiguously (a line runs lengthwise through each row). Column store: five column blocks c1..c5 stacked; each row is one cell in every column block (vertical lines R1, R2, R3 run down through all five blocks).

questions.q: What 'naive' mental model did the teacher give for how a column-oriented database stores data?
questions.answer: One separate file per column; line 1 of each file holds that column's value for row 1, line 2 for row 2, and so on.

questions.q: What analytics query was used as the example, and which columns does it really need?
questions.answer: SELECT avg(price) WHERE ts = '...' (average stock price for a day); only two columns, price and ts (timestamp).

questions.q: Why is a row store inefficient for that query even if you don't SELECT the other columns (board: 100-column table)?
questions.answer: It goes row by row reading all columns and discarding the unneeded ones (98 of 100 on the board): the engine must skim symbol, name, exchange to find row boundaries, wasting disk IO.

questions.q: What does a column-oriented database read for such a query?
questions.answer: Only the columns that are part of the query (the price and timestamp files); it does not even skim the others - no disk IO for them.

questions.q: Where are column-oriented databases used? Name the examples given.
questions.answer: Massive analytics and data warehouses: Amazon Redshift, Google BigQuery; also columnar file formats like Parquet.

questions.q: Why should you not build a blogging application on a column-oriented database?
questions.answer: Transactional apps almost always read the whole row (e.g. render a user profile = select * of 10-15 columns), so the column layout gives no benefit; columnar wins only when you pick a few columns out of hundreds/thousands.

questions.q: Which paper did the teacher strongly recommend reading on column stores?
questions.answer: 'C-Store: A Column-Oriented DBMS' - the foundational paper on column-oriented databases.

questions.q: In a row-oriented database, when you SELECT only some columns, does the disk read only those columns?
questions.answer: No. It reads all the columns of the row from disk, then picks the ones you need and sends them. A column store doesn't read unneeded columns (think separate files).

questions.q: A drawback raised was that inserts are heavy in column stores. How are column stores used in practice because of this?
questions.answer: They are never the primary database. The primary copy lives in a traditional DB (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, DynamoDB), and a job ingests data into the column-oriented data warehouse just for analytics.

questions.q: Why do column stores need much less space, and what compression gain did the teacher say is normal?
questions.answer: Each column holds homogeneous data (similar, discrete values), so it compresses very heavily; about 29x is a normal gain he sees.

questions.q: Which compression techniques did the teacher name as working well on columnar data?
questions.answer: Huffman, Snappy, LZ compression; and he told students to read about run-length encoding. (Discrete values like symbols can be stored as small codes.)

questions.q: Are column-oriented databases priced per read/write operation like many cloud NoSQL databases?
questions.answer: No. They run continuously; you pre-provision capacity (reserved capacity) and pay for the servers, not on-demand per operation.

questions.q: What common belief about graph databases did the teacher call the worst way to think about them, and what example illustrated it?
questions.answer: That any use case you can visualise as a graph should use a graph DB. Example: modelling Twitter's follow/following relationship on a graph DB could be catastrophic (really expensive); it is a trivial use case.

questions.q: How do graph databases store data, according to the teacher?
questions.answer: Nodes and edges - literally the adjacency-list representation from a data-structures course, with data APIs exposed on top; they specialise in graph algorithms.

questions.q: What LinkedIn feature was given as an example of a sophisticated graph algorithm?
questions.answer: Showing how far a person is from you - 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th degree connection.

questions.q: Why are graph databases a poor fit for storing something simple, and what analogy did the teacher use?
questions.answer: They are very hard to scale and extremely memory intensive (many built on legacy stacks). Using them just to store follow/following data is like using the Hulk to open a glass jar. Use them when you need core graph algorithms.

questions.q: Explain the collaborative-filtering example with the iPhone and AirPods.
questions.answer: Users who bought the same product (iPhone node) form a cohort of similar users. If one of them buys AirPods, Amazon recommends AirPods to everyone else in the cohort. Real systems go 2-3 levels deep.

questions.q: In the Grammarly/HDFC story, how does a graph database detect a suspicious transaction?
questions.answer: Each person has a graph of their transactions (e.g. all domestic). An international payment creates a new edge outside that closely knit cluster - it sticks out like a sore thumb - so a suspicion score is computed and the bank calls the customer to approve.

questions.q: How many parameters and what latency budget did the teacher cite for fraud detection at financial companies?
questions.answer: About 50-60 parameters (country, region, product type, ...) ingested into a per-person graph; the decision must be made within a 200 ms SLA (from a JP Morgan Chase VP of engineering).

questions.q: What graph database examples were given?
questions.answer: Neo4j (one of the first), Amazon Neptune, Dgraph (written in Go; falters a bit at high scale; embedded DB BadgerDB), TigerGraph (proprietary, used by many financial companies).

questions.q: What three reasons did the board give for 'Why non-relational DBs scale', and what was written beneath them?
questions.answer: No relations; data can be denormalized; data is modelled to be sharded. Beneath: 'We can also achieve [these] on SQL databases' - so saying SQL does not scale is not entirely correct.

questions.q: How do foreign-key constraints ensure correctness in a relational database? Give the insert and delete cases.
questions.answer: With a non-null foreign key you cannot insert a row unless the referenced row exists; and a parent row cannot be deleted until all its child rows are deleted.

questions.q: What is the 'backstory' of why relational databases chose correctness over scale?
questions.answer: Their first use cases were financial, where correctness/strong consistency of data mattered more than performing at scale or high ingestion.

questions.q: How can you make a relational database partition like a non-relational one?
questions.answer: Don't use foreign keys/constraints; without them you can shard the data exactly how a non-relational database does.

questions.q: Reproduce the board's two lists 'When to use SQL?' and 'When to use NoSQL?'.
questions.answer: SQL: ACID; relations, constraints; fixed schema. NoSQL: no relations; data can be denormalized; data can be sharded.

questions.q: When should you pick SQL, and does the SQL database guarantee correctness automatically?
questions.answer: When data correctness/strong consistency (ACID) is the most important feature. It gives you the tooling (foreign keys, check constraints) but you have to apply them.

questions.q: When should you pick NoSQL? Give the examples of workloads the teacher listed.
questions.answer: Gigantic data with very high ingestion where correctness is not critical (losing an attribute is okay): messages (Instagram), posts, logs, metrics. Databases like Cassandra give sharding/partitioning out of the box and drop constraints.

questions.q: How is a graph database's adjacency list stored internally, per the teacher's blunt picture?
questions.answer: On disk (not only in memory) via a storage engine, serialized simply - think of each node's neighbours as a comma-separated list of IDs; depends on the database.

questions.q: What did the teacher mean by 'the KV store is the NAND gate of databases'?
questions.answer: Just as every logic gate can be built from NAND gates, every database can be modelled on top of a key-value store (maybe not as performant).

questions.q: Are graph databases used transactionally by user-facing applications?
questions.answer: No. You ingest data into them asynchronously and derive something (e.g. fraud signals, recommendations) out of it.

questions.q: Why is a graph database better than a relational one for an N-level-deep query? Give the three reasons.
questions.answer: A graph traversal answers it in one simple query. In SQL you need N self-joins, rewriting the query per depth (painful); N self-joins on huge data are not optimal; and relational data sits on one node whereas graph DBs give distribution out of the box.

questions.q: MongoDB offers ACID now. What caveat did the teacher give?
questions.answer: Cross-shard ACID is implemented with distributed transactions, which slow down throughput; the official docs say to use it sparingly. Within a single shard ACID is easy to guarantee.

questions.q: Is 'key-value' a type of storage engine? Contrast Redis and DynamoDB.
questions.answer: No - KV is an access pattern; it does not define the underlying store. Redis implements it in memory, DynamoDB on disk.

questions.q: If you have a KV access pattern, what options do you have besides building it on a relational database?
questions.answer: Use a specialised KV store like DynamoDB or Redis; decide based on the features you need (e.g. correctness).

questions.q: Will a KV store on a relational DB, DynamoDB and Redis all scale the same? Give the teacher's example.
questions.answer: No; it depends on what you store, access pattern, throughput, partitioning/sharding. E.g. storing blobs of ~4 MB each would make a relational DB 'cry', while DynamoDB would work better.

questions.q: What were the four requirements for Slack's real-time communication?
questions.answer: Multiple users, multiple channels; users DM or message in a channel; real-time chat; historical messages can be scrolled through.

questions.q: What similar systems can be built with the same architecture?
questions.answer: Multiplayer games, real-time chat, interactions, real-time polls, creator tools, etc.

questions.q: Does writing a schema with tables and attributes mean we are using a relational database?
questions.answer: No. The schema is just entities and attributes; the database is picked later based on the guarantees needed.

questions.q: Why did the teacher prefer the name 'membership' over 'user_channel' for the user-to-channel mapping table?
questions.answer: Name entities as nouns: it gives the table a persona and makes it natural to add columns. 'user_channel' is just a mapping name (what would you call a 3-way mapping? user_channel_message?).

questions.q: First proposal: messages table with both channel_id and receiver_id (one of them null). What are its problems?
questions.answer: One column is always null, and allowing nulls means a glitch can insert a row with both null - an orphan row.

questions.q: Why not use two separate tables, one for channel messages and one for direct messages?
questions.answer: Migrations get harder: adding a new attribute to messages means changing both tables.

questions.q: Why is a single 'to' column with prefixed IDs (e.g. 'ch-…' / 'usr-…') a poor design?
questions.answer: Every query needs string processing to decide whether to join with channels or users; you can't write efficient queries.

questions.q: Why is 'to' plus a 'type' enum (channel/user) still not good enough?
questions.answer: You cannot put a foreign key on 'to' because it may point to either table, and business logic fills up with if/else branches.

questions.q: Why must a message store where it is going (a destination column)?
questions.answer: Otherwise you cannot render all the messages of a channel.

questions.q: What is the final modelling of DMs, and how does Slack's own API confirm it?
questions.answer: A DM is a channel with 2 people. In the Slack API, to DM a user you first create a channel with that user and then post in it; the UI renders it as a DM.

questions.q: What general schema principle did the DM-as-channel decision illustrate?
questions.answer: Look for a generalised way to store things rather than special cases; piggyback on existing entities; ifs and elses are the worst in databases.

questions.q: Give the final data model drawn on the board (four tables and their fields).
questions.answer: users(id, name); channels(id, org, name, type: grp/user/reg); Membership(user_id, channel_id, [checkpoint]); Messages(from, channel_id, created_at, msg). Note: DM = channel with 2 people.

questions.q: What is the channel 'type' used for?
questions.answer: To render it differently in the UI: DMs in the bottom half, channels in the top half (types group/user/regular).

questions.q: In order, how did the Messages table evolve on the board before reaching its final form?
questions.answer: sender_id / channel_id / receiver_id / msg (-> DM or ch) -> from / to (-> ch/usr) / msg -> from / to / type: ch/u / msg (to pointing back to channels) -> from / channel_id / msg (then created_at added).

questions.q: What is the 'checkpoint' in the membership table and what does it enable?
questions.answer: Where the user last read up to in that channel (a timestamp or message ID, depending on granularity). It drives unread counts and jumping to the last-read point; it moves to the bottom when the channel is opened.

questions.q: What other attributes can go into membership thanks to naming it as a noun?
questions.answer: Anything about how a user interacts with a channel: muted, favorited, notification preferences, last active time - no need for a separate favorites table.

questions.q: What two key takeaways from the schema part did the teacher state?
questions.answer: Name entities as nouns (membership), and piggyback on existing entities (DM = channel) instead of if/else special cases.

questions.q: Which database did the teacher choose for Slack messages, and why is fancy NoSQL not required?
questions.answer: Any database that can be sharded/partitioned; even a simple sharded relational DB (MySQL) works, as would MongoDB/Cassandra. Enterprise message volume is not very high (people are at work, not chit-chatting).

questions.q: For which product would the teacher have chosen Cassandra, and why?
questions.answer: Instagram Messenger: everyone chit-chats, very high ingestion, all users in one DB, so a high-ingestion database like Cassandra fits. Product requirements, not stack affinity, decide.

questions.q: A student wanted to send messages over the WebSocket 'because we already have it' for receiving. What was the teacher's response?
questions.answer: Just because you have it doesn't mean you should use it; think about the guarantees you gain or lose. Receiving must use WebSocket, but sending can go via the API.

questions.q: Why is 'Slack has frequent communication, so save the per-message overhead with WebSocket' a weak argument?
questions.answer: Slack messages are not as frequent as Instagram chat; for an enterprise customer persistence of messages matters more than saving overhead. If overhead were decisive the whole world would use WebSocket for everything and REST would not exist.

questions.q: What observable behaviour hints that Slack sends messages via a normal API call rather than instantly over a WebSocket?
questions.answer: When you hit send, the message first shows grey and then turns black - a visible delay, so it is not extreme real time.

questions.q: On the '3 ways to persist the message' diagram, what do markers 1, 2 and 3 label, and which product does each represent?
questions.answer: 1 = the API servers path (persist in DB, then notify the edge server) - Slack; 2 = the Kafka pipe with workers writing to DB - hypothetical WhatsApp; 3 = the Edge Server (WS only, no persistence) - Zoom chat. Caption: 'Depending on criticality of persistence we pick one over other'.

questions.q: What is an 'edge server' in this design?
questions.answer: A WebSocket server (fancy name). Not a CloudFront/CDN edge server - the normal servers that hold the users' WebSocket connections.

questions.q: Why must Slack persist a message before broadcasting it to the channel?
questions.answer: For an enterprise, broadcasting an unsaved message hurts credibility: people could misquote you ('I received this message') while it never got stored. So Slack does synchronous persistence first.

questions.q: Describe the Slack (type 1) message flow.
questions.answer: User sends via normal HTTP to the API server; it persists in the database; then sends the message/event to the WebSocket (edge) server, which delivers it to users in real time. Send over HTTP, receive over WebSocket.

questions.q: In the hypothetical WhatsApp (type 2), how is a message sent and persisted, and why is that acceptable?
questions.answer: Sent over WebSocket to the edge server, which pushes it to Kafka and immediately relays it to the other user; workers later persist (batch write) to the DB asynchronously. Acceptable because a copy already lives on the user's device and WhatsApp needs speed, not a persistence guarantee.

questions.q: Why would the Kafka (asynchronous) route be a bad idea for Slack?
questions.answer: If persistence takes, say, 10 minutes, users are notified but on refresh they don't see the message because reads come from the database, which doesn't have it yet. Slack users refresh/scroll channels from the DB.

questions.q: What is the third type of communication and its example?
questions.answer: No persistence at all, only real time: Zoom chat. Leave and rejoin and you see no history; anyone connected gets the message and that's it.

questions.q: Give the reasons for not making DB calls from the WebSocket (edge) server.
questions.answer: Security: it is exposed to the internet and would hold DB credentials. Load: it already handles many TCP connections. Blast radius: if it goes down, all real-time features break. Companies keep it a relay (at most pushing to an async queue).

questions.q: Why did the teacher reject sending messages via UDP over TLS (with WebSocket only for receiving)?
questions.answer: Weak guarantees and many retries, the client would have to handle broadcast (who tells B?), and client code becomes needlessly complex for a micro-optimisation. UDP is for cases where dropping data is OK, not Slack messages. Keep it simple: simple systems scale.

questions.q: Do WebSockets offer 'persistence'? Clarify.
questions.answer: They give a persistent connection, not database persistence. Slack needs data stored; doing it from the WebSocket server means it talks to the DB (load, security, risk).

questions.q: What is the most an edge server should hold, from a security standpoint?
questions.answer: At most a Kafka connection string to push messages - never database credentials, since edge servers are the most vulnerable servers in the infrastructure.

questions.q: In the first high-level sketch (A, B, API, WS, DB), what lines were added to show the Slack flow?
questions.answer: A line from the API stack to the DB cylinders (MySQL / Cassandra / Mongo) and a vertical line joining the API stack and the WS stack: API persists, then tells the WebSocket servers.

questions.q: Why does the final architecture diagram use the Kafka route even though Slack was explained with synchronous persistence?
questions.answer: Deliberately conflicting: any implementation is possible depending on the guarantees; there's no single converged design, to make students think about each decision.

questions.q: What does it imply when a product uses WebSockets / persistent connections?
questions.answer: They power its most critical features (e.g. Discord chat); the expensive persistent TCP connection gives low-latency communication without re-establishing connections.

questions.q: What simplifying assumption and channel setup were used to explain scaling WebSocket servers?
questions.answer: Each WebSocket server handles at most 4 connections. Channel 1 has 5 users A-E: A-D connect to WS1, E must connect to WS2.

questions.q: How does a WebSocket server know which users are connected to it?
questions.answer: The WebSocket library (e.g. Socket.io) keeps track of connected users via the handshake.

questions.q: How does a WebSocket server learn which channels its users belong to?
questions.answer: On connecting, the user sends meta information - its membership (e.g. A -> C1, C2, C3). The server keeps it in memory (WS1: A->C1, B->C1, C->C1, D->C1; WS2: E->C1).

questions.q: How is the WebSocket server kept up to date when a user joins or leaves a channel, and what consistency does that give?
questions.answer: The user sends the change, and also periodically re-sends its membership; the server is kept eventually consistent with membership.

questions.q: When A sends a message to channel 1, whom does WS1 deliver it to locally?
questions.answer: B, C and D (members of C1 connected to WS1) - not back to A.

questions.q: Why did the teacher push back on adding Kafka/a messaging service to get the message from WS1 to WS2?
questions.answer: It slows things down and needs consumers running; start simple first.

questions.q: What is the simplest way to get A's message to E on WS2, as drawn on the board?
questions.answer: A plain TCP connection (not WebSocket) between WS1 and WS2. WS1 sends the message over it; WS2 sees it's for C1, finds E and sends it to E.

questions.q: When user F of channel 1 connects to WS3, how was it connected in the drawing?
questions.answer: Another TCP link, from WS1 to WS3 (diagonal labelled TCP); WS3 delivers to F. Adding servers leads to a full mesh where every server connects to every other.

questions.q: Students suggested problems like server failure and sending messages to servers that don't need them. Why weren't these 'the overhead'?
questions.answer: A server down is a fault-tolerance issue, not overhead; unneeded sends can be optimised with a global state. The real overhead was something bigger 'staring at you'.

questions.q: Is there a TCP three-way handshake for every message sent between WebSocket servers?
questions.answer: No; the TCP connection is established once and messages are just relayed over it.

questions.q: What is the real overhead of the mesh of WebSocket servers?
questions.answer: Each server has limited connections/ports; in a mesh every server holds a persistent TCP connection to every other, hogging connections meant for users. E.g. 4 users + 3 inter-server links = 7 connections, 3 of which are just inter-server.

questions.q: What replaced the mesh, and how many inter-server connections does each server then need?
questions.answer: A real-time Pub/Sub (like Redis, not Kafka - Kafka would slow it down); each server holds just one connection to it (e.g. 4 for A-D + 1 to Pub/Sub).

questions.q: What does a real-time Pub/Sub guarantee and not guarantee?
questions.answer: It pushes a message to everyone subscribed at that moment, with zero persistence: it doesn't store the message or guarantee delivery; a server not connected at that moment simply doesn't receive it.

questions.q: Why distinguish Redis channels from Slack channels, and why shouldn't a C1 message go to every server?
questions.answer: Both are called 'channels'. A message for Slack channel C1 should only go to servers that have C1 members (e.g. WS2), not WS3/WS4.

questions.q: Who subscribes to the Redis Pub/Sub channel - the user or the server? When does it happen?
questions.answer: The WebSocket server, not the user. When a user connects and tells its membership, the server fires a Redis SUBSCRIBE for those channels (e.g. WS1 -> SUB(C1), WS2 -> SUB(C1)).

questions.q: Trace A's message to channel C1 in the final Pub/Sub drawing (WS1 with A-D, WS2 with E and F, WS3 with G and H in C2).
questions.answer: A -> WS1 -> delivers to B, C, D; WS1 publishes to Redis for C1; Redis pushes to WS2 (subscribed to C1), which sends to E and F. WS3 (only C2 members G, H) does not get it.

questions.q: Does the receiving WebSocket server pull messages from Redis Pub/Sub?
questions.answer: No, Redis pushes the message to subscribed servers.

questions.q: What if one Redis Pub/Sub isn't enough, and how do you reduce its load?
questions.answer: Run a sharded cluster with intelligent balancing; and try to put users of the same set of channels on the same WebSocket servers.

questions.q: How does a user find which WebSocket server to connect to?
questions.answer: It asks a balancer service ('Balance Connections') first, which returns the server's IP; then the user connects to it. Like DNS, but not DNS.

questions.q: What naive balancing strategy did the teacher suggest, and why is it effective?
questions.answer: One WebSocket server per organisation: tens of thousands of employees is nothing for a WebSocket server. Then messages stay within one server and nothing needs to go through Redis.

questions.q: What happens if a WebSocket server goes down?
questions.answer: Users reconnect, ask the balancer again and get another server's IP; the balancer moves them. Meanwhile some messages may flow through Redis; it can also periodically rebalance to minimise Redis IO.

questions.q: What hands-on exercise did the teacher strongly recommend?
questions.answer: Write a hello world with Redis Pub/Sub (local Redis server, a few clients) - also WebSocket and the balancer - to see it doesn't persist and pushes messages.

questions.q: In the recap, how is the message store sharded and why?
questions.answer: Large number of messages -> sharded DB (any DB you can shard, even SQL). Shards are mutually exclusive and sharded by channel_id, so all messages of a channel are in one DB: scrolling is simple, no cross-shard query.

questions.q: In the recap's formal data model, what tables are listed?
questions.answer: workspace(id, name); channels(id, workspace_id, name, type); messages(id, channel_id, message, user_id, ts); membership(channel_id, user_id, checkpoint). Insight: DMs are channels with 2 people, so only channels need modelling well.

questions.q: Describe the 'very basic flow' for sending a message.
questions.answer: send_message(from_user, to_channel, text) via a REST call to a Messaging Service (load balancer -> API servers); the API server finds the shard by channel_id and stores the message in the partitioned DB. Works for both DMs and channels.

questions.q: In the recap, the three persistence types were matched to colours. Which?
questions.answer: Synchronous storage = Slack (white); asynchronous storage = WhatsApp (green); non-persistent = Zoom (blue).

questions.q: What client-side connection limit did the teacher highlight, which browsers have which values, and why does it exist?
questions.answer: Browsers allow at most ~6 concurrent TCP connections per domain (6 Chrome, 8 Firefox), to prevent abuse such as DDoS.

questions.q: Explain the 100-images example for the connection limit.
questions.answer: With no WebSocket, a page with 100 images loads 6 at a time. With one WebSocket open, only 5 at a time; with two, 4 at a time - each WebSocket permanently uses one of the 6 slots.

questions.q: Because of this limit, how many WebSocket connections should a product open, and what goes over it?
questions.answer: Just one; multiplex all real-time communication (chat, live video hearts, notifications) over it. A fleet of edge servers holds these connections.

questions.q: What did the edge-server fleet diagram say about other services that need to reach users in real time?
questions.answer: Any service (chat, notification, etc.) that wants to talk to users in real time sends the info through these edge servers.

questions.q: Describe the overall architecture diagram: what connects to what?
questions.answer: Users -> WS -> Edge Servers (holding membership); Edge Servers <-> Redis PubSub [clustered] <-> other Edge Servers; Edge Servers -> Kafka -> Messaging Service Workers -> Messages DB (partitioned); users -> load balancer -> API Servers -> DB for non-realtime API (channel scroll, muted channels). A Balancer tells users which edge server to use.

questions.q: Which persistence level does the overall architecture use, and what goes over REST vs WebSocket?
questions.answer: Level 2: asynchronous persistence via Kafka. Real-time over WebSocket/edge servers; historical scrolling and other non-real-time reads over normal HTTP to the messaging/API service.

questions.q: What 'Insight' did the board state about asynchronously persisted messages?
questions.answer: Messages once sent will always be persisted - there will be no DB-level runtime exception like a unique key failure.

questions.q: Which use cases were listed as non-real-time (served by REST)?
questions.answer: Channel scroll, DM scroll, unimportant messages loaded when the channel is clicked (e.g. muted channels) - anything messaging-related that is not 'pushed'.

questions.q: Redis Pub/Sub may lose real-time messages. What remedies were given?
questions.answer: We can't drop messages: a correction job / periodic background refresh (e.g. JS thread fetching the last 50 messages, like WhatsApp's 'checking for new messages'); the channel-scroll REST API loads them when clicked; or buffer messages in another Kafka and replay when sockets are back.

questions.q: In the edge-server internals recap, what three steps does the edge server take when A sends to B on the same server?
questions.answer: 1. Persist the message in Kafka; 2. Find B in the local connection pool; 3. Send the message to B. (Socket.io manages which user is connected and how to reach it.)

questions.q: In the recap of scaling edge servers, what sequence of ideas was written for getting A's message to E on Edge Server 2?
questions.answer: 5th user forms a WebSocket with another server -> message reaches E only if it reaches Edge Server 2 -> 'We bridge the gap' with a TCP connection -> but with 100 edge servers, every server to every other is not a great idea -> do better: Realtime PubSub.

questions.q: In the edge-server subscription example (A in c1,c2,c3; B in c2,c4,c5; C in c1,c3; D in c4), what does the edge server subscribe to?
questions.answer: SUB(c1,c2,c3,c4,c5) - the union of its users' Slack channels; one Pub/Sub channel per Slack channel (noted 'can be optimized').

questions.q: What actually is an edge server in implementation terms?
questions.answer: A normal WebSocket server running a Node.js Socket.io process.

questions.q: Should edge server IPs be exposed directly to clients or put behind a load balancer? Give the trade-off.
questions.answer: Both are fine. A load balancer adds a hop (connections stay sticky: user->LB, LB->server), about 3-5 ms latency per hop. For ultra-low latency (e.g. live class streaming), expose IPs directly; big companies do.

questions.q: If you expose edge servers to the internet, how do you secure them?
questions.answer: Strict security review: change route tables, hide ports, block SSH, etc. Put zero credentials on them - no DB connection; at most a Kafka connection string to an internal Kafka.

questions.q: If an exposed edge server is compromised, what's the worst case and the mitigation?
questions.answer: Nothing critical is there; worst is DDoS, which a simple rate limiter can prevent.

questions.q: How do edge servers learn about channel changes (new channel, join/leave)?
questions.answer: The user does the action (API call -> DB update); a notification is broadcast via Redis Pub/Sub to edge servers; affected clients are notified over WebSocket and tell their edge server 'I'm now in channel 3'; the edge server updates its in-memory store and subscribes in Redis. Clients also periodically re-send membership.

questions.q: What alternative to the client telling its membership was given, and when can it be used?
questions.answer: The edge server periodically pulls membership from the backend API; only if the server is private/internal, not on a publicly exposed server.

questions.q: Why Redis Pub/Sub specifically?
questions.answer: Any real-time Pub/Sub works - the requirement is real-time push to all subscribers; the teacher used Redis to build this exact system.

questions.q: Do Redis Pub/Sub messages have an expiry?
questions.answer: No expiry and no persistence: nobody stores the message; it's sent to current subscribers.

questions.q: Since membership comes from clients, how do you prevent a bad actor from claiming membership of a private channel?
questions.answer: A client could falsely claim membership and receive messages (man-in-the-middle). For critical info, make the edge service private behind a load balancer and have it get channel membership from the backend (DB or periodic API call).

questions.q: Why not have a separate service tell the edge server whom to send each message to?
questions.answer: A network call per message is too slow and not real time; the edge server can keep this info itself.

questions.q: In this design, what is guaranteed and what isn't?
questions.answer: Persistence is guaranteed (more important for enterprise); real-time notification is not (may be lost in Redis), but users see it on refresh.

questions.q: With many organisations and channels, how is the Redis Pub/Sub kept manageable?
questions.answer: Redis is a cluster, and the balancer keeps users of one organisation on one edge server, so cross-server traffic via Redis is minimal (worst case only).

questions.q: How do Redis Pub/Sub and Kafka differ? Is either superior?
questions.answer: Kafka: pull-based (consumers pull), persists history. Redis Pub/Sub: pushes to connected subscribers, zero persistence. Neither is superior: Redis for real time, Kafka for persistence.

questions.q: In the Kafka route, if workers persist a message a day late, is the message delivered a day late?
questions.answer: No: delivered immediately in real time; only storage is delayed, so a refresh won't show it until it's persisted.

questions.q: What is the 'best' way to build today's system?
questions.answer: There's no best way; choose based on the guarantees you give customers ('a buffet; make your own plate').

questions.q: For a multi-level-marketing hierarchy, is a graph DB better?
questions.answer: Yes if queries go 3/5/10 levels deep: in a relational DB that needs many self-joins (10 levels = 9 self-joins), which is messy.

questions.q: How would message deletion work in the WhatsApp vs Slack variants?
questions.answer: WhatsApp (stores nothing): send a delete event and remove it from users' local storage. Slack: delete in the DB via the API, then notify users in real time it's deleted.

questions.q: Why did deletion take WhatsApp long? What numbers did the teacher give?
questions.answer: Scale, product decisions, staggered rollouts. With this architecture, backend changes would be ~100-300 lines. His own real-time text chat took 3.5 months with a 3-engineer team.

questions.q: If two messages arrive out of order at the receiver, what are the simple fixes?
questions.answer: Render as received, and on refresh order comes from the DB (source of truth). Or keep client state sorted by timestamp and insert out-of-order messages in the middle.

questions.q: What could cause duplicate or out-of-order messages in Teams, and how does order eventually fix itself?
questions.answer: Broadcasting before persisting, or retries on the WebSocket server. Fixed by refresh or a background job (e.g. every minute fetch the last 50 messages and reorder).

questions.q: Which timestamp defines message order?
questions.answer: The DB insertion time (database clock), not the client's.

questions.q: Why never trust client-sent timestamps?
questions.answer: A user can change their clock (e.g. to 1 January 1970); the DB time is the source of truth.

questions.q: What's the theoretically correct ordering solution, and why not use it?
questions.answer: Vector clocks per client (CRDT-style merge conflict resolution). Too complex and slow; not worth it for an edge case.

questions.q: How do you avoid losing a message if a DB node fails mid-write?
questions.answer: Use a replicated distributed DB (replication factor 3): the write is acknowledged only after it's on 3 storage nodes (like DynamoDB). Workers don't write to 3 DBs themselves; they hold the message and retry until the DB commits.

questions.q: Is it OK for workers and API servers to share the same database?
questions.answer: Yes; routing worker writes through the API adds a needless network hop. He dislikes the database-per-microservice anti-pattern.

questions.q: Why keep a channel type instead of just private/public?
questions.answer: To differentiate a DM from a 2-person private channel: you can add people to a channel but not to a DM; they render differently, and it's extensible.

questions.q: Is the 6-connection limit per domain shared across subdomains like mail.google.com and chat.google.com?
questions.answer: No; it's per hostname: 6 for Gmail, 6 for Chat, 6 for Meet, etc.

questions.q: When a Slack user returns from vacation, are old messages relayed over WebSocket? How does it differ from WhatsApp?
questions.answer: No; Slack shows unread counts (via membership checkpoint) and loads messages over the API. WhatsApp must deliver them to the device since messages live there.
